hints: Focus on how solubility changes down Group 2, hydroxides and sulfates trend in opposite directions.
Remember that $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is almost insoluble while $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$ is much more soluble, so one needs far less $\text{OH}^-$ to precipitate.
Now flip it for sulfates, $\text{MgSO}_4$ is very soluble while $\text{SrSO}_4$ is insoluble, so think which sulfate hits its limit first.
walkthrough:
**Recall the two Group 2 solubility trends**

Think trends, not memorised facts for one compound. Hydroxides get more soluble down the group. Sulfates get less soluble down the group.

$$\text{solubility of M(OH)}_2: \text{Mg} < \text{Ca} < \text{Sr} < \text{Ba}$$
$$\text{solubility of MSO}_4: \text{Mg} > \text{Ca} > \text{Sr} > \text{Ba}$$

**Decide what precipitates first with NaOH**

Both $\text{Mg}^{2+}$ and $\text{Sr}^{2+}$ start at the same concentration. Adding $\text{OH}^-$ dropwise will exceed the solubility limit of the less soluble hydroxide first.

$$\text{Mg}^{2+}(aq) + 2\text{OH}^-(aq) \rightarrow \text{Mg(OH)}_2(s)$$
That is magnesium hydroxide, because $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is far less soluble than $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$.

**Decide what precipitates first with H2SO4**

Adding $\text{SO}_4^{2-}$ dropwise will exceed the solubility limit of the less soluble sulfate first. $\text{MgSO}_4$ is soluble in water, $\text{SrSO}_4$ is insoluble.

$$\text{Sr}^{2+}(aq) + \text{SO}_4^{2-}(aq) \rightarrow \text{SrSO}_4(s)$$
That is strontium sulfate. So the pair is magnesium hydroxide and strontium sulfate.

options.A: Half right, half wrong. Magnesium hydroxide is correct for NaOH, as it is less soluble than strontium hydroxide. But magnesium sulfate is wrong for H2SO4 because $\text{MgSO}_4$ is soluble and stays in solution, while $\text{SrSO}_4$ is insoluble and precipitates first.
options.B: Correct on both sides. With NaOH, the less soluble $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ precipitates before the more soluble $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$. With H2SO4, the insoluble $\text{SrSO}_4$ precipitates before $\text{MgSO}_4$, which is soluble. This matches the opposite Group 2 trends.
options.C: Wrong on both sides. It reverses both trends. Strontium hydroxide is more soluble than magnesium hydroxide, so it precipitates later, not first. Magnesium sulfate is soluble, so it does not precipitate first ahead of strontium sulfate.
options.D: Half right, half wrong. Strontium sulfate is correct for H2SO4, as sulfates become less soluble down the group. But strontium hydroxide is wrong for NaOH because hydroxides become more soluble down the group, so $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ precipitates first, not $\text{Sr(OH)}_2$.
